terms.gloss: figurative, used in a transferred sense (of a word)
evidence: Cic. Or. 27.92: trānslāta dīcō … quae per similitūdinem ab aliā rē … trānsferuntur (Lewis & Short s.v. trānsferō)
Quint. 8.3.24: cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta
terms.comment: A word carried over to another sense by likeness, verbum trānslātum: Cicero’s and Quintilian’s term, against proprium. A metaphor is trānslātiō (Cic. de Or. 3.38.156, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Ascon. ad Cic. Verr. 2.6 (Lewis & Short s.v. figūrō)
terms.comment: Traupman’s adverb (propriē an figūrātē?, 239). Quintilian’s figūrātus is said of speech made with figures of speech (9.1.13), not quite of a word used in a transferred sense.

evidence: Isid. 17.6.23 (Lewis & Short, for the adverb trānslātīvē)
terms.comment: In Cicero and Quintilian a term of rhetoric for a plea that moves a case to another court; the sense “metaphorical” is Isidore’s, for the adverb.

evidence: Cic. de Or. 3.37.149: words quae trānsferuntur (Lewis & Short s.v. trānsferō)
terms.comment: Adverbial phrases for “figuratively”: by metaphor, in transferred words.

phrases.english: when some word is carried over more boldly
Why? — Because it is used for “war”.

sources: Lewis & Short: transfero · Lewis & Short: figuro · Lewis & Short: translativus · Lewis & Short: translatio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 239, p. 246.
